source: Plot luminosity against temperature to sort stars into the main sequence, giants and white dwarfs.
Students forget that temperature increases to the left on an H–R diagram.

Around 1911 to 1913, Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell each plotted stars by two numbers: their spectral class (temperature) and their luminosity. Instead of a random scatter, the stars fell into a few distinct groups. This Hertzsprung–Russell (H–R) diagram is the most useful picture in stellar astronomy.

Why must cool, luminous stars be huge, and hot, dim ones tiny? Because of luminosity, size and temperature: $L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$. A star on the right is cool, so each square meter gives off little light; to be very luminous it must have an enormous surface. A star at the lower left is hot, so each square meter is very bright; to be dim overall it must be very small. Lines of equal radius run diagonally across the diagram: supergiants hundreds of times the Sun's radius, white dwarfs about the size of Earth.

On the H–R diagram, luminosity increases upward and temperature increases to the left. Main-sequence stars lie on a diagonal band; giants sit above it to the right (big), white dwarfs below it to the left (small).
The H–R diagram: a few hundred stars of a realistic population, with some well-known stars named.
A star has the Sun's temperature but is $400$ times as luminous. How big is it, and where does it sit?
$20$ solar radii, in the giant region.
Same temperature as the Sun (class G), but far above the main sequence: a giant.
A star is $10{,}000$ times dimmer than the Sun ($L = 0.0001$) and twice as hot. How big is it?
About $1700$ km: a white dwarf at the lower left.

On almost every other graph, values increase to the right. On the H–R diagram temperature increases to the left, a tradition from when the axis was spectral class (O, B, A … M). Read the axis labels before reading a position. Check: blue O stars and the hot white dwarfs are on the left, red M stars and red giants on the right.
